text.brief: On April 1, 2001, Lieutenant Shane Osborn landed a damaged EP-3E on Hainan Island after a fighter of the People's Liberation Army Navy struck it over the South China Sea.
text.record: The fighter's pilot, Wang Wei, died in the collision. The Party held the twenty-four crew members for eleven days and released them after Washington delivered a letter that said sorry twice, once for his death and once for the landing without clearance ([Letter from Ambassador Prueher to Chinese Foreign Minister Tang, April 11, 2001 (Bush White House archive)](https://georgewbush-whitehouse.archives.gov/news/releases/2001/04/20010411-1.html)). The crew had destroyed part of the plane's classified equipment and data before landing, and a Navy review found the destruction incomplete. The Party returned the aircraft in pieces aboard a Russian cargo plane that July ([CRS report RL30946: China-U.S. aircraft collision incident of April 2001 (via EveryCRSReport)](https://www.everycrsreport.com/reports/RL30946.html)).
text.reading: The Party turned an accident that followed its pilot's aggressive intercepts into a demand for an apology, and it presented Washington's wording at home as a confession. It also held the aircraft long enough to study what the crew could not destroy, which is Stratagem 5.
text.gapText: Data Architecture. The aircraft carried more classified material than its crew could destroy in the minutes before landing.
text.fix: Carry only the data a mission needs, and build destruction into the equipment rather than leaving it to a crew in an emergency.
